claims.text: An aluminum-containing high-entropy alloy can achieve lower density while maintaining or improving overall mechanical performance compared with traditional alloys.
Integrating simulation, experimental validation, and iterative alloy design can accelerate the development of high-performance HEAs.
The precursor is a multi-principal-element HEA containing aluminum.
The precursor is intended to form a predominantly single-phase solid solution.
The proposed intervention optimizes alloy composition and processing through iterative feedback between simulations and experiments.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering can control phase evolution, refine microstructure, and improve mechanical properties in the proposed Al-containing HEA.
The alloy is to be evaluated at ambient and elevated temperatures relevant to structural applications.
Controlled processing will produce a refined microstructure containing homogeneously distributed nanoscale precipitates.
Controlled phase evolution may produce a dual-phase lamellar structure.
Simulation-guided iterative design can refine phase stability and microstructure.
Composition and microstructure optimization reduces the alloy's overall density.
Controlled strengthening precipitates can increase alloy strength.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates can preserve or enhance ductility by facilitating dislocation transmission and relieving stress concentrations.
The optimized microstructure will provide enhanced thermal stability.
The optimized alloy will have a density at least approximately 10% below that of conventional alloys.
The optimized alloy will provide comparable or superior strength and ductility at operational temperatures.
The baseline may be either a conventional aluminum alloy or a standard HEA produced without integrated simulation-experiment design.
Excessive formation of intermetallic phases could negate the proposed density benefit.
Processing may cause undesirable phase segregation or chemical clustering in an Al-containing HEA.
A simulation-guided sample can be compared with a conventionally processed control under identical density, mechanical, thermal, and microstructural tests.

contradictions.description: The principal hypothesis and predicted outcome emphasize comparison with traditional or conventional alloys, whereas the proposed decisive experiment primarily compares simulation-guided and standard processing. These comparators test different causal questions, and the control is not specified consistently.
